$comment: Why each family is in the pool, and who said so. data/pool.json decides WHAT the season grades; this file records WHY that choice is defensible, with a citation per claim. It exists because the pool's own justification was mechanical - a scenario was in because some benchmark author had banded it - and 'an author put it in a tier' does not answer 'is this a good measure of dynamic clicking'. Nothing reads this at runtime: it is documentation held to the same standard as code, which is what npm run validate:rationale is for. Every number quoted here is re-derived from data/scenario_taxonomy.json rather than trusted, and every family in the pool must appear.
$evidence: Three kinds, in descending order of what they can settle. A benchmark author's published design note is the strongest: it says what the scenario was built to isolate, in the words of the person who built it. KovaaK's own in-game scenario description is next, and is first-party for scenarios no benchmark documents. Community discussion is last and is used only where it says something the other two do not - which is mostly about scenarios that predate the benchmarks that later adopted them. Where a family's evidence is thin, this file says so rather than padding it: 'thin' is a fact about the pool worth being able to see.
$audience: plays and entries are KovaaK's own counters for the named scenario, copied from data/scenario_taxonomy.json and checked against it. They are here because 'the community plays this' is a claim that should carry a number. Read entries as people who have posted a score and plays as runs; the least-played scenario in the pool has 13,262 plays, so nothing here is obscure.

kovaaks-scenario.title: KovaaK's scenario metadata, author-written descriptions
kovaaks-scenario.note: Mirrored into data/scenario_taxonomy.json; the description quoted is the author's own.

steam-ts-thread.title: Which are the best Target Switching Scenarios? - KovaaK's General Discussions

families.isolates: Static clicking over long travel, at a sensitivity the scenario itself argues against lowering.
families.why: Two claims have to hold for a static family: that it measures clicking rather than pathing, and that it does not quietly reward a sensitivity nobody plays at. Voltaic built ww5t for the second, and the Wide Wall lineage above it is the oldest and most-played static test in the game - 5,601,340 plays on the top-window variant alone, which is more evidence about what a static score means than any benchmark can supply.

evidence.says: Medium targets on a curved, exceptionally wide spawn region, designed "to discourage the use of very low sensitivities".

families.isolates: Static clicking where accuracy is enforced by the ammo economy rather than by a score curve.
families.why: The second static family deliberately measures the same skill under a different scoring rule. Square-root accuracy lets a fast spammer trade precision for volume; a reload clip does not, because a miss costs more ammo than a hit returns. Two static families that both reward spam would be one family measured twice.

evidence.says: 1wXts is "low target count and on the smaller side for small static targets to minimise pathing and to increase focus on pure static technique".
The reload mechanic replaces square-root accuracy with a modified ammo system forcing higher accuracy: misses cost more than hits restore.

families.isolates: Clicking a target that is moving diagonally and continuously - aiming while tracking.
families.why: Pasu is the scenario the phrase 'dynamic clicking' is usually pointing at, and Voltaic kept it across seasons while fixing what was wrong with it. Its scoring is the interesting part: square-root accuracy is applied specifically to stop the scenario paying for spam, which is the failure mode that would make a dynamic score mean nothing.

evidence.says: Diagonally moving targets; the air-jump bug and awkward wall interaction were fixed, and it "uses square root accuracy to balance the tendency for Pasu to be a more spam heavy clicking scenario".

families.isolates: Clicking targets whose direction changes on a bounce, so the timing is read rather than followed.
families.why: Pasu's targets move predictably once read; a bouncing target resets that read every time it hits a surface. Pairing them keeps the sub-skill from resting entirely on how well a player has learned one movement pattern.

evidence.says: The author's description: "Four single-click bots leap in mid-high arcs on top of a flat surface, changing depths as they traverse. The player's weapon has three shots and empty magazines recover in their entirety upon each elimination." - the arc and the depth change are what make the timing a read rather than a follow, and the three-shot magazine is what stops it paying for spam.

families.thin: The hardest windows here are the least documented in the Clicking pool. Voltaic dropped Bounceshot after S4 rather than replacing it, so there is no current design note for the lineage above Novice.

families.isolates: Clicking small targets on a predictable horizontal path, weighted toward precision over speed.
families.why: Linear clicking is the bridge between static and dynamic, and it splits into a precision half and a speed half. This is the precision half, and Voltaic says so explicitly - small targets and square-root accuracy, against Frogtagon's speed focus.

evidence.says: Heads strafing horizontally with a vertical bob; it "focuses more on precision, so the targets are fairly small and square root accuracy is used".

families.isolates: Linear clicking at speed, where the cost is the travel between targets rather than the shot itself.
families.why: The speed half of linear clicking. Frogtagon opens it because Voltaic tuned it for exactly that, and the vox lineage above it is the widely-played wide-angle version of the same question.

evidence.says: Frogs moving in straight lines, offering "predictable strafes" with intuitive bounce timing, "intended to be more speed focused".

families.isolates: Repeated short flicks between two close targets, under a reload clip.
families.why: Micro clicking is the sub-skill Voltaic's nine do not name, and it is not static clicking made smaller: the limiting factor is the correction at the end of a very short flick, not target acquisition. The smallflicks lineage is the community's standard test of it and long predates the benchmarks that adopted it.

evidence.says: Two close small targets that respawn instantly - practice for micro corrections, micro flicking and cluster work.

families.isolates: Micro clicking on a target that is also moving, so the correction is against a shifting point.
families.why: Smallflicks holds the static half of micro clicking; this holds the moving half. Grading micro on two static scenarios would measure one skill twice and leave the harder version of it unmeasured.

evidence.says: A Pasu-derived scenario scaled down to micro distances, so the target moves while the correction is being made.

families.thin: The Entry variant that opens this family has 13,262 plays, the smallest audience in the pool. It is used because it is the only novice-tier micro scenario the 43-benchmark corpus contains.

families.isolates: Holding a crosshair on a small target moving smoothly and predictably.
families.why: The purest precise-tracking test in the pool: predictable movement, so what is being measured is how steadily the crosshair is held rather than how well the movement is read. That separation is the whole reason Precise and Reading are different sub-skills here.

evidence.says: A smoothly moving bot with no direction changes to react to, which is what isolates holding from reading.

families.isolates: Precise tracking where the target's speed changes, so a learned rhythm stops working.
families.why: Smoothbot can be beaten by settling into the target's rhythm. Voltaic built Snake Track specifically to stop that, which makes the two a genuine pair rather than a duplicate: one measures the hold, the other measures the hold when the rhythm is taken away.

evidence.says: A thin snake with accelerating and decelerating strafes, which prevents pure centering and forces "a higher focus on tracking and less on rhythm".

families.isolates: Reacting to direction changes in the air, where there is no floor to constrain the movement.
families.why: Reactive tracking is about the cost of a direction change, and air targets make that cost highest because the change can come on any axis. Voltaic rebuilt Aether for movement variety rather than difficulty, which is the right property for the novice end of a reactive ladder.

evidence.says: Aerial strafes both vertical and horizontal, with greater movement variety than typical Air variants and an emphasis on reactivity.

families.isolates: Reacting to horizontal-only strafes, which is the shape an actual duel takes.
families.why: The counterpart to the air family, and the more transferable of the two: enemies in most FPS titles strafe on a plane. Voltaic's Ground exists precisely to hold the horizontal-only case apart from the free-movement one.

evidence.says: Horizontal strafes only, inspired by Plink Plaza; the distinction from the air scenarios is the horizontal-only focus.

families.isolates: Sustained tracking of a target circling at varying distance, with conventional strafing.
families.why: Control tracking is the long-hold case: the target does not try to break the track, it simply keeps moving, and the score is how much of the time the crosshair was on it. Controlsphere is the most-played scenario in the entire pool at 10.9 million plays, which makes it about as close to a community standard as a scenario gets.

evidence.says: Aerial strafes in a circular arena; it "focuses less on forward and backwards movement and also has more conventional strafing behavior".
The author's description: "Tracking a small gently jumping dot as it flies around you at varying distance and speed."

families.isolates: Control tracking on all three axes, including movement toward and away from the player.
families.why: Controlsphere deliberately plays down forward and backward movement; this family is where that movement is the point. The Whisphere variants sit here rather than in Precise on Voltaic's own authority: they name whisphere as one of the two scenarios Controlsphere was derived from, which places it in the same lineage rather than a neighbouring one.

evidence.says: "Designed to focus on XYZ tracking with a target that doesn't collide with the walls."
Controlsphere is described as inspired by 'cloverrawcontrol' and 'whisphere', which is what puts Whisphere in the control lineage.

families.isolates: Tracking where the difficulty is predicting where the target goes next, not holding the crosshair steady.
families.why: Reading is the second sub-skill Voltaic's nine do not name, and separating it from Precise is what stops a smooth-hands player and a good-reads player getting the same tracking rank for different reasons. Air Voltaic is the long-standing test of the reading half.

evidence.says: An air target whose strafe pattern is unpredictable enough that the limiting factor is the read rather than the hold.

families.isolates: Reading strafe direction changes at close range, where the angular speed is highest.
families.why: The close-range half of reading. These are among the oldest scenarios in KovaaK's and were the community's standard tracking routine long before any benchmark adopted them - the reason the top-window variant still carries 761,427 plays without appearing in a current benchmark tier.

evidence.says: The author's description is "Close Fast Strafes, but the bots are invincible" - the invincible variants exist so the score is time-on-target over a fixed period rather than a kill count.
Easy-to-read movement, used in community routines specifically for smoothness work rather than reading difficulty.

families.thin: Two of this family's variants are among the three scenarios in the pool for which KovaaK's publishes no aim type and no benchmark tier settles one, so their category rests on the pool's own classification. The author descriptions above are what supports it.

families.isolates: Switching between static targets, where all of the cost is the travel and none is the track.
families.why: The cleanest possible speed-switching test: the targets do not move, so the only thing being measured is how fast the crosshair gets to the next one and stops. Voltaic built it as their first static target-switching scenario for that reason. The Expert variant is psalmTS rather than a DotTS variant, and that is the point of it: Voltaic retired PsalmTS in S5 by replacing it with EddieTS specifically to get more regular and predictable movement, which makes the scenario they moved away from the less predictable member of the same lineage - the right thing to ask at the top of a speed ladder, and a claim from the author who made it.

evidence.says: Static dots with a notably longer time-to-kill than Pokeball scenarios - their first static target switching scenario.

EddieTS is introduced as a replacement for PsalmTS with "more regular and predictable movement, to lean into the speed target switching design" - so PsalmTS is the same lineage with the predictability taken out.

families.isolates: Speed switching across wide angles, where the travel is long enough to dominate the shot.
families.why: DotTS holds the short-travel case; the vox lineage holds the wide one, and the community treats it as the wide-angle switch-speed reference. Voltaic's EddieTS opens the family because it was rebuilt specifically to be predictable, which is what a speed test wants at the novice end. voxTS Viscose Varied grades the Intermediate window rather than the Expert one: Aimerz+ SpeedTS runs the same twelve scenarios at both its difficulties, so its Hard listing asks a higher score of the same scenario rather than naming a harder one, and reading it as difficulty had this scenario grading Expert while the only other source that names it said Intermediate.

evidence.says: A replacement for PsalmTS with "more regular and predictable movement, to lean into the speed target switching design".
Recommended in community discussion for speed switching specifically, as against the evasive long-TTK scenarios in the same thread.

families.isolates: Switching onto targets that are actively evading on all three axes.
families.why: Evasive switching is where the target does not cooperate: acquisition is only half the job and the other half is staying on it. Voltaic's FlyTS is built around unpredictable strafe directions and a long time-to-kill, which is exactly that split, and it carries the family through three windows. The Expert variant is domiSwitch, the best-evidenced placement in the pool: four independent sources - Aimerz+, both Viscose seasons and snakbox - all file it in their hardest tier, none of them lists it twice, and it is one of the two scenarios the community names when asked what trains evasive switching. The other is tamTargetSwitch Smooth, which the Smooth Switching family grades, so the sub-skill's two families are the two scenarios people actually point at.

evidence.says: "Heavier focus on XYZ movement with a fairly high TTK, with the bots strafing in less conventional and predictable directions."
Named alongside tamTargetSwitch Smooth as an "evasive long TTK" scenario that emphasises landing accuracy and post-flick micro correction, which the thread calls "pretty pivotal for good TS".

The author's description is "55 hp, regen after 0.3 seconds without damage" - a regenerating health pool makes the score depend on staying on the target after the flick rather than on reaching it, which is the property the sub-skill is named for.

families.thin: KovaaK's classifies this scenario Clicking, and it is the one place in the pool where Apogee overrules a first-party source. It is overruled on a measurement rather than an opinion: domiSwitch fires 177 shots per kill at a regenerating target, against the 1.1 to 1.3 every clicking scenario in the corpus produces. The correction and its re-derivation live in data/aim_type_corrections.json and npm run validate:aimtypes. Worth knowing because aim_type is the column find-match partitions the queue on, so if the correction were ever dropped this scenario would be graded as Switching and matched as Clicking.

families.isolates: Switching where holding the target after the flick is what scores, not the flick.
families.why: The clearest statement of the evasive half, and the one the community makes itself: the regenerating-dot scenarios pay for what happens after the flick lands. That is the property the sub-skill is named for, and it is why this family sits beside FlyTS rather than under Speed.

evidence.says: Recommended as an "evasive long TTK" scenario that emphasises landing accuracy and post-flick micro correction, which the thread calls "pretty pivotal for good TS".
The author's description: small regenerating dots circling the player, 0.5s TTK, regeneration starting immediately on going off target.

families.isolates: Switching onto small, slow targets where precision rather than speed is the limit.
families.why: Stability switching is the third switching sub-skill, and it is the one that is not about speed at all. Voltaic describes ControlTS as DriftTS with the emphasis moved to precision, which is the distinction the sub-skill exists to hold.

evidence.says: Gently jumping targets, similar to DriftTS but with "greater focus on precision, so the targets are slower and smaller".

families.isolates: Switching between close targets, where the flick is short enough that stability dominates.
families.why: The short-range half of stability switching, and the family that sits closest to micro clicking without crossing into it - the author says as much. Penta Bounce opens it because Voltaic built it for predictable straight-line movement at varying angles, which is the novice form of the same question.

evidence.says: Targets ricocheting inside a pentagon, built as a "smoothness target switching scenario with predictable movement in straight lines at varying angles".
The author's description: "1w2t Smallflicks and voxTS had baby, and they named it beanTS" - explicitly a cross of the micro-clicking and switching lineages.

families.thin: beanTS is one of the three pool scenarios KovaaK's publishes no aim type for, so its category cannot be checked against the game and validate:pool warns about it. Two things settle it instead. Its sibling beanTS Larger carries the same author description and IS classified Target Switching by KovaaK's. And the two measure the same mechanic: 28.5 shots per kill against 26.4, both with a lightning gun, over more than nine thousand and seven thousand kills respectively - a one-shot clicking scenario would be near 1.1. The method is the one described in data/aim_type_corrections.json; there is no correction to make here, because KovaaK's has said nothing to contradict.

families.isolates: Dynamic clicking where the next target appears the moment the last one dies, so the cost is reacquisition rather than holding an aim.
families.why: Popcorn is the dynamic-clicking lineage the corpus agrees on, and the agreement is strongest exactly where the ladder needs it. Voltaic rates it at every tier from Novice to Elite, which supplies three of the four windows from one author. The Expert rank is scored on Popcorn MV Advanced instead of Voltaic's own Elite variant, and that is a deliberate swap: four independent benchmarks name Popcorn MV Advanced at their hardest tier where only Voltaic names its Elite one, and the boards are 4,511 against 1,028. A rank set on the smaller board could not separate its own top two ranks - both cleared by 0.09% - which is a rank nobody can hold.

evidence.says: Voltaic's S5 and S5.5 sheets both carry Popcorn, and agree on its Novice and Intermediate numbers.
Viscose S2 files Popcorn MV Advanced at Expert; Viscose, Jade Palace and snakbox each place it at their own hardest tier.
Jade Palace Dynamic rates Popcorn MV Advanced Hard, the fourth independent author to name it at the top.

families.isolates: Precise tracking on a small target that keeps moving, where the score is time on target rather than a flick landed.
families.why: Precise Tracking carried two families and needed a third that was not another sphere. PGT is Voltaic's own precise-tracking lineage across all four of its tiers, so every window is one author's opinion of the same skill rather than four authors' opinions stitched together, and its Novice board is the largest of any scenario entering the pool at 208,370 entries. Its Expert board is the thinnest thing here at 1,727, which clears the floor and is recorded rather than hidden.

evidence.says: Voltaic S5 and S5.5 both rate PGT, and disagree by under 2% at Advanced - the numbers are reconciled to the median.
The author's own description files it under precise tracking.

families.isolates: Reactive tracking against a target that changes direction without telegraphing it, so reading the change is the whole cost.
families.why: Plaza is Voltaic S4's reactive lineage and the one scenario in the corpus that four authors place in the reactive band. Its first three windows come from S4 unchanged. The Expert rank moved off VT Plaza Elite, whose board carries 324 players, onto VT Plaza Viscose Thin at 4,420 - a rank read off three hundred people is a fact about them rather than about the skill, which is the same objection this pool already records against its thinnest sources.

evidence.says: Voltaic S4 rates Plaza from Novice to Advanced, supplying the first three windows from one author.
Aimerz+ Reactive Tracking files VT Plaza Viscose Thin at Hard, which is what bands it to Expert.

families.isolates: Control tracking with the target's movement unsmoothed, so a correction has to be made continuously rather than once per pass.
families.why: Control Tracking's two families were Controlsphere and Raw Control, both of which reward a settled crosshair. RawControlSphere is Viscose's lineage across Entry, Easier, Medium and Hard, which makes it the only control family whose four windows are one author's graded progression. The Expert rank is scored on RawControlSphere Hard rather than the Expert-tier scenario of the same name: 1,897 players against 710, and the thinner board is not worth the tier's label.

evidence.says: Viscose S2 rates the RawControlSphere lineage at Entry, Easier, Medium, Hard and Expert - every window this family needs.
The author's description marks it as the unsmoothed variant of Controlsphere.

families.isolates: Reading tracking in the air, where the target cannot be killed and the only score is how much of its path was followed.
families.why: Reading Tracking is the sub-skill the old two-per-sub-skill rule left thinnest, and Air Voltaic Invincible 4 is the most-agreed reading scenario outside the pool - five independent benchmarks name it. Unlike every other family added here its Expert board is not thin at all: it was the only one of the seven candidates whose top window cleared the old percentile-derived board requirement as well as the floor that replaced it, and the only one that needed no substitution at Expert to do so.

evidence.says: Viscose S2 rates the Invincible 4 lineage at Easier, Medium and Expert; Viscose Entry supplies the Novice window.
Jade Palace Air files Air Voltaic Invincible 4 at Hard, agreeing on where the top of the lineage sits.
